title: Trapezium rule estimate
what_it_asks: You are given a function or a table of values, often with a diagram of the curve. You are asked to estimate an integral using strips of equal width. You may then reuse the estimate for a related integral, judge whether it is an over- or underestimate, or compare it with the exact value. The idea is that each strip is treated as a trapezium, so the curve is replaced by straight-line tops.
typical_structure: Usually two or three parts, sometimes four. The first part is often a short completion of the table of values, worth one or two marks. The next part applies the rule and is typically the largest, about three or four marks. A later part reuses the estimate (scaling it, or using a log law or constant factor), comments on accuracy, or asks for the exact integral to compare. Later parts often lean on the earlier estimate or table.
mark_pattern: Most parts mix independent marks with one method and one accuracy mark. The usual sequence is B1 M1 A1. The B1 is for the correct strip width or a correct table value. The M1 is for a trapezium bracket with the right structure. The A1 is for the value to the required accuracy. Table completion is usually B1 or B1 B1, one mark per value. A 4-mark part is often B1 M1 A1ft A1, where the A1ft follows your own table values. Reuse or exact-integration parts are usually M1 A1 or M1 A1 A1: a method mark for the scaling or integration, then accuracy. A comment on over- or underestimate is typically a single B1.

where_marks_leak.text: Many students give the estimate to the wrong number of decimal places or significant figures. The final A1 is lost even when the method was right.
Many students treat the number of ordinates as the number of strips, so $h$ is wrong. The M1 for the bracket can go, and the A1 that depends on it goes too.
Many students double the end ordinates or leave out the factor $\frac{h}{2}$. The M1 is lost, and the A1 after it with it.
You round table values or a partial sum, and the final answer drifts outside the accepted range. The A1 is lost.
In the exact integral, you multiply by the old power or add 1 wrongly to a negative or fractional power. The M1 for integrating is lost, and the A1 marks after it.

write_to_earn: Write $h$ as the interval length divided by the number of strips before you use it, so the B1 is secured.
Write the bracket as first plus last, plus twice the middle values, with $\frac{h}{2}$ in front, before you put in numbers.
Keep full calculator values in the table and round only the final answer to the accuracy asked.
For a reuse part, say which factor or log law links the new integral to your estimate, and then apply it.
For an over- or underestimate comment, refer to the curve shape (concave or convex) and say whether the tops lie above or below the curve.
